Name: defense_secrets
Title: Defense Secrets: Arms of Deceit
Experiment: Setting: Japan’s Ministry of Defense is holding an emergency closed-door session about a controversial export deal for next-generation weapons. Unknown to most attendees, bribery, illegal transfers, and foreign espionage are already in motion.  Factions: (1) Integrity Bloc – career officials, inspectors, or watchdog politicians who must expose the conspiracy and keep state secrets safe; (2) Conspiracy Bloc – crooked procurement officers, defense-industry lobbyists, and embedded foreign agents who want the transfer to go through and the paper trail erased.  Core Loop: Each day consists of (a) Plenary Debate – open discussion where new “Leak/Event” cards are revealed (e.g., ‘Redacted Contract Page Found’, ‘Overnight Database Crash’); (b) Accusation Vote – players nominate someone for dismissal or arrest; (c) Night Ops – Conspiracy Bloc secretly chooses one illegal action (bribe, data wipe, scapegoat, etc.), while special Integrity roles investigate.  Roles & Abilities: • Internal Inspector (peek at one player’s night action log without revealing how you obtained it) • Watchdog MP (may publicly subpoena one document, forcing a chosen player to reveal one secret card) • Corrupt Procurement Chief (can plant forged approval stamps, framing an innocent) • Arms Lobbyist (can spend ‘Funds’ tokens to buy silence, blocking one accusation) • Foreign Agent (once per game may extract a classified file, advancing Conspiracy victory track).  Legal Emphasis: Rules and flavor text reference Japan’s Three Principles on Arms Exports, the 2014 Transfer Guidelines, and the Act on the Protection of Specially Designated Secrets; revealing too much classified info in open debate triggers a penalty that can aid the Conspiracy Bloc.  Win Conditions: Integrity Bloc wins by eliminating all Conspiracy members or sabotaging the export license; Conspiracy Bloc wins if the export is approved OR if classified data is stolen. Debrief sheets link every in-game mechanic to real scandals such as the Lockheed bribery affair and recent JMOD bid-rigging cases, turning post-game reflection into a mini-seminar on defense-sector compliance.

Name: black_money_bank
Title: Black Money: The Washing Game
Experiment: Setting: A high-profile Tokyo bank branch where rumors of large-scale money laundering swirl after a sudden spike in international wire transfers.  Factions: (1) Clean Bankers – honest staff aiming to protect the bank’s reputation and report suspicious activity; (2) Washers – insiders colluding with yakuza fronts to clean dirty cash; (3) Opportunists – gray characters (e.g., sales-obsessed loan officers) who can swing either way.  Game Flow: A round has three phases: (i) Morning Briefing – players receive daily transaction logs (mini-ledgers) with hidden anomalies; (ii) Staff Meeting – open debate, rule-book references to Japan’s Act on Prevention of Transfer of Criminal Proceeds, FATF audits, and KYC procedures are encouraged; (iii) After-Hours – Washers secretly pick laundering maneuvers from a deck (‘Layer funds’, ‘Send to HK shell’, ‘Smurf deposits’) while the Compliance Officer audits one log, the IT Examiner checks access history, and the New Hire can whistle-blow anonymously.  Mechanics: • Each account has a risk score; if risk crosses a threshold, regulators intervene (automatic Clean Banker progress). • Washers collect ‘Cleanliness Tokens’ by successfully executing layered transactions over multiple nights. • The Compliance Officer’s report is phrased in regulatory language – too vague and colleagues may ignore it, too direct and Washers will target them. • If an employee is fired by vote, their private ledger cards are revealed, teaching real red-flag patterns (e.g., round-number transfers, mismatch between economic profile and volume).  Legal Emphasis: Players must cite sections of the Criminal Proceeds Regulation Act, Suspicious Transaction Report obligations, and recent FATF Mutual Evaluation criticisms; accurate citations grant bonus credibility tokens.  Win Conditions: Clean Bankers win by blocking the launderers’ token track or dismissing all Washers; Washers win by reaching the required laundering volume first.  Post-Game Debrief: A facilitator sheet maps every action to genuine cases (e.g., 2024 remittance routing arrests) and underscores why AML compliance, KYC, and STR filings matter in Japanese banking.

Name: corporate_whistle
Title: Corporate Whistle: Shadows in the Balance Sheet
Experiment: Setting: The executive suite of a listed electronics giant days before its annual earnings release. Whispers of fraudulent accounting ripple through the ranks after an anonymous email hints at billions hidden off the books.  Factions: (1) Reformists – executives, auditors, and employees committed to truthful reporting and regulatory compliance; (2) Cover-Up Crew – those complicit in the fraud who will do anything to keep the façade intact; (3) Fence-Sitters – managers terrified of the fallout who may be swayed by either side.  Rounds: • Board Session – players debate quarterly figures while ‘Audit Questions’ cards (e.g., ‘Why is inventory turnover doubled?’) surface; each statement can be challenged, forcing the speaker to place a Credibility or Doubt token. • Voting – the board may suspend one member or decide to delay disclosures. • Night Work – Cover-Up Crew executes one covert action: falsify ledgers, threaten a whistle-blower, or bribe an external auditor; Reformist roles (Internal Control Officer, External Auditor, Anonymous Whistle-blower) gather evidence.  Evidence Engine: A central timeline board tracks altered ledgers. If the timeline shows too many discrepancies, regulators (simulated by event cards) step in. The Whistle-blower can drop a ‘Leak Bomb’ once per game, sending partial evidence to media; doing so raises public pressure but exposes their identity.  Role Highlights: • CFO (fraud mastermind) can redirect suspicion by presenting complex but opaque financial jargon. • Internal Control Officer may secretly compare any two ledger entries for inconsistencies. • External Auditor sees one random ledger before the night ends. • HR Head can shield a player from retaliation, representing the revised 2022 Whistleblower Protection Act requirements for safe reporting channels.  Legal Connections: Dialogue references the Companies Act, J-SOX internal control rules, Financial Instruments and Exchange Act penalties, and real scandals (Olympus, Toshiba). Over-the-top attempts to silence whistle-blowers result in an automatic +1 risk with the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission track.  Win Conditions: Reformists win if they expose the fraud (enough discrepancies proven) or remove all Cover-Up Crew; Cover-Up Crew wins if they survive through the earnings call or discredit whistle-blowers.  Educational Overlay: The facilitator notes link each token or action to governance best practices, illustrating how internal controls, external auditing, and whistle-blower protections work in the Japanese legal environment and why ethical leadership matters.
